passage:
Avni: Everyone says you were the only one who walked out. How?

Yamini: Honestly, I didn't walk out at first. What helped was that I kept ordinary things going. Every Sunday I still called home, and I still had dinner with my old roommate on Wednesdays. After each meeting I told them what the group had said. One night I repeated a line the leader liked, "doubt just means your ego is talking." My roommate laughed and said, "How convenient for whoever is saying it." I heard it from outside for the first time. The group kept telling me my family didn't understand me, but the calls sounded so normal, so unhurried, next to the meetings. That gap kept showing me what was off.

qa.q: How often did Yamini call home?
How did Yamini feel when the roommate laughed at the leader's line?
qa.a: Yamini was startled, then clearer: hearing the line from outside made it sound different.

qa.q: What else could Yamini do to keep a clear view, and why?
qa.a: Yamini could write down what the group asks for and compare it with what family and friends think, because a written record is harder to explain away.

qa.q: How might the roommate have felt hearing Yamini's updates?
qa.a: The roommate probably felt worried but glad to be trusted, and helped just by listening and asking plain questions.

grounding: Illustrates keeping weekly calls with family and old friends and discussing the group's claims with them, so outside views break the closed loop.

passage:
I'm Naveen, Manoj's older brother. When Manoj joined a meditation community in Bengaluru in his second year, Amma worried. I worried too, especially when he said they encouraged "cutting noise" from outside.
But every Sunday at seven he still called us. And he didn't just chat. He'd say, "They told us this week that exams don't matter if your mind is clear. What do you think?" Amma would laugh and say, "Your mind can be clear and you can still pass." He'd laugh too.
Another week he said, "They want me to move into the community house." I asked why. He said, "They say it's more focused." Then he said, "I don't know, what do you think?" We talked for an hour. He stayed in the hostel.
He also met two old school friends every month, whatever happened. I don't know everything he felt, but those calls kept him with us.

qa.q: At what time did Manoj call every Sunday?
qa.a: He called at seven every Sunday.

qa.q: What might Manoj have been feeling when he asked, 'What do you think?'
qa.a: He may have felt unsure and doubtful about what the group was telling him, and trusted his family to help him check it.

qa.q: What else could help Manoj keep an outside view?
qa.a: He could write down anything the group says that feels off and bring it to his monthly meetings with school friends too.

qa.q: How does Manoj's approach look to Naveen?
qa.a: Naveen was worried at first but sees the weekly calls and open questions as what kept Manoj connected and thinking for himself.

grounding: Shows the person keeping weekly calls with family and meeting old friends, and checking what the group says with them, breaking the group's closed loop.

First week of September. Arnab joined a "leadership circle" at his college. The seniors were friendly, the talks inspiring. They also said, often, that "outsiders won't get it."
Mid-September. Arnab noticed he had skipped his Sunday call home twice. He set a phone alarm: Sunday 8 p.m., call Maa. He also texted his school friend Omkar: "Chai every Friday? Non-negotiable."
October. At Friday chai, Arnab told Omkar what the seniors had said that week: that grades don't matter and members should give their scholarship money to "the mission". Omkar frowned. "That sounds like they want your money." That Sunday, Arnab told Maa too. She asked quietly, "Would your teachers agree?"
November. Arnab still went to one talk a month. But he had stopped believing everything the seniors said, and he didn't give them a rupee. "Friday chai saved me," he told Omkar.

qa.q: What time was Arnab's Sunday call alarm set for?
qa.a: It was set for 8 p.m. on Sundays.

qa.q: What did Arnab likely feel when he noticed he had skipped two calls home?
qa.a: He likely felt uneasy and a little guilty, which is why he set an alarm and fixed a weekly chai with Omkar.

qa.q: What else could Arnab do if the seniors push harder?
qa.a: He could talk to a teacher or college counsellor along with Maa, since an adult on campus can help if pressure grows.

qa.q: How does Omkar see what the group was saying?
qa.a: Omkar sees it plainly as a push for Arnab's money, and his blunt view helped Arnab step back.

grounding: Shows the person keeping calls with family and meetings with an old friend, and discussing the group's claims with them to break the closed loop.
